title: Sport in Zendia
intro: You should spend about 20 minutes on this passage.

paras.t: Sport is changing in every country, but the changes are not always simple. The imaginary country of Zendia, whose sports councils have kept careful records for forty years, shows how different activities can follow quite different paths. This passage examines four of them: running, tennis, cycling and swimming. For each one, it asks what happened, and then why. The answers help to explain what governments can and cannot do to encourage people to take exercise. The records are unusually complete, because every club and public pool in the country must report its numbers each year, and because the same definitions have been used since the 1980s.

Running is the clearest success story. In 1985, only a few thousand people in Zendia took part in organised races. Since then the number has risen without a break, and it now exceeds two million. The reasons are easy to see: running needs no club, no special place and almost no equipment, and free weekly timed races in public parks have made it easy for beginners to join. Doctors have also encouraged it, since regular running protects the heart.

The history of tennis has been less happy. Membership of tennis clubs was high in the 1980s, but it has fallen at every count since. Courts are expensive to build and to maintain, and in cities they take up land that developers want for housing. Many clubs have closed. Young people, who once learned the game at school, now have a wide choice of other sports, and the television coverage of tennis has moved from free to paid channels, which has reduced its audience.

Cycling shows the most unpredictable pattern. The number of people who cycle regularly goes up and down from one year to the next. It rises in years when the national tour passes close to large towns, and when the price of fuel is high. It falls after wet summers, and after accidents that attract much attention in the newspapers. Because the numbers move in this way, planners find it difficult to decide how many cycle paths to build, and some have given up trying.

Swimming has followed yet another course. Until 2012, the number of regular swimmers was stable, at around three million. Then two of the biggest public pools in the capital closed for repairs that were meant to last a year but in fact took four. The number of swimmers fell abruptly and has not recovered, since many of those who stopped have found other ways of exercising. The council has promised to open new pools, but the work has not started. Swimming teachers say that many children now reach the age of ten without learning to swim, which they regard as a serious risk to safety as well as to health.

What can be learned from these cases? Dr Hana Weiss, a sports economist, argues that policy should be guided by the nature of each activity. Sports that need little equipment, such as running, grow almost by themselves if the government provides safe places and information. Sports that depend on special buildings, such as swimming and tennis, need steady investment, and a short closure can do lasting damage. Sports that depend on weather, such as cycling, will always change with the season, and planners must accept this.

Looking ahead, the sports councils of Zendia are planning more flexible schemes. Instead of building one large centre, they hope to offer smaller facilities in more neighbourhoods, and to give people simple ways to try new activities. They also plan to count participants more accurately, using electronic cards, since the present figures depend on surveys that people do not always answer honestly. If the plans succeed, the next forty years may be more encouraging for the less fortunate sports.
